newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU backs jobs, but whose idea was it?.
newsitem.headline: EU backs jobs, but whose idea was it?.

text.p: When Britain's former employment secretary Norman Tebbit told a Conservative party conference the unemployed should get on their bicycles and look for work, there was outrage at his callousness.
This week Europe's leaders got on their bikes and talked into the night about work. Worker mobility and flexibility were no longer outrageous, they were shared beliefs.
The bicycles were gifts from the Dutch summit hosts. But unravelling whose idea it was to shift Europe's focus onto job creation was not so easy.
Britain's new Labour administration, the new champion of the flexible labour markets introduced by the defeated Conservatives, said it had thought it all up.
Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown said his initiative on jobs unveiled last week to European finance ministers in Luxembourg had caught the imagination.

"What I think has happened over the last few days is that jobs have moved to the centre of the European agenda," British Prime Minister Tony Blair said, thanks, he added, to the new "British initiative".
But the Germans, with whom Blair found common ground in refusing to agree to spend any extra European money to pay for grandiose job creation projects, begged politely to differ.

"Employment is not new on the European agenda nor is it on it for the first time. The process...began (at the 1994 EU summit) in Essen and was continued six months ago (at the EU summit) in Dublin," said German Finance Minister Theo Waigel.

France's new socialist government, swept into power on June 1 on a wave of anger at austerity measures imposed to ready the country for entry into Europe's planned single currency, said it forced a reluctant EU to focus on jobs and growth.
The French delayed agreement a week ago on a pact to limit budget deficits and demanded a balancing resolution to help Europe's 18 million unemployed.

"This is just a start, but we've only been in office for 10 days. We have started to reverse a trend. We have loosened the noose," said French socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's spokesman, Manuel Valls.
But France's claim was immediately disputed by the Italians.
"Last year I made the proposals that the French are making now, said Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi.
"They are the proposals that Italy made at Florence... I was left alone (at the 1996 EU summit) in Florence, the only one of 15 to be suggesting this."
Others cited their even earlier efforts.
Greece's Deputy Foreign Minister George Papandreou said the Greeks put forward job proposals at the 1955 Madrid summit.

Scandinavian countries joined in. Sweden claimed it launched the idea of focussing on jobs in 1995. "The resistence has gradually faded away...the development has proved Sweden right," said Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson. Denmark too claimed authorship.
One of the few countries not to claim authorship of the jobs plan was Luxembourg.

But, in true European tradition, the tiny European country may end up the one state permanently remembered for the drive for jobs which leaders say is essential if public support for Europe's is to be boosted.

One of the concrete proposals agreed by EU leaders was to hold a special summit in the next six motnhs, when Luxembourg holds the bloc's rotating presidency. If any jobs plan emerges, it will doubtless be known as the Luxembourg employment programme.
